Title: A review of principles in design and usability testing of tactile technology for individuals with visual impairments
Authors: Emily L. Horton; Ramkesh Renganathan; Bryan N. Toth; Alexa J. Cohen; Andrea V. Bajcsy; Amelia Bateman; Mathew C. Jennings; Anish Khattar; Ryan S. Kuo; Felix A. Lee; Meilin K. Lim; Laura W. Migasiuk; Amy Zhang; Oliver K. Zhao; Marcio A. Oliveira
Problem addressed: No consolidated principles for designing and testing personal tactile devices for visually impaired (VI) users.
Target population: Studies (1980-2014) of personal electronic tactile devices tested with at least one VI user.
Methodology: Systematic-style review: EBSCO databases, 300 unique records -> 148 after title/abstract -> 62 included; dual-reviewer cross-checking; standardized extraction matrix.
Technology: Pin matrices, force-feedback devices, accessible touchscreens.
Main findings: Multimodal (tactile + audio) feedback usually works best for complex information; iterative user-centred design with VI users at every stage is best practice; test with at least ~5 VI users; sighted (often blindfolded) users appear in 19 studies and are not an effective substitute for VI users. Application areas: education (26), navigation (19), computer access (10).
Limitations: Restricted databases and date range (to 2014); personal electronic devices only (passive tactile labels excluded); many included studies had very small VI samples.
Research gaps: Passive, non-electronic tactile markers for household controls are outside its scope.
Relevance to SPARSH: Supports SPARSH's evaluation design: involve blind users, not just blindfolded proxies; target >=5 VI participants for formative usability.
Design implications: Pair tactile caps with an audio/voice channel in the setup guide; plan iterative testing with blind users; report sighted-proxy results only as pilot data.

Title: Evaluating the Use of Tactile Shapes in Associative Learning for People Who Are Blind
Authors: Richa Gupta; Steve Mannheimer; P. V. Madhusudan Rao; Meenakshi Balakrishnan
Problem addressed: Whether simple 2D tactile shapes help blind people encode, retain and recall labels associated with them.
Target population: Students at schools for blind students in Indianapolis (USA) and New Delhi (India).
Methodology: Four recall experiments with verbal and tactile cues; labels grouped as consonant, dissonant or abstract relative to shape.
Technology: Simple raised 2D tactile shapes; Braille verbal cues.
Main findings: Consonant (meaningfully matched) labels were recalled best; Braille verbal cues outperformed tactile-shape cues; tactile shapes need not resemble visual referents; simple shapes support long-term retention; primacy and distinctiveness effects observed. Authors recommend standardized tactile symbol sets and simple tactile images.
Limitations: School-age sample; lab recall tasks rather than everyday use; sample sizes not verified.
Research gaps: No study of shape-to-function codes for home controls.
Relevance to SPARSH: Strong support for SPARSH's small, arbitrary-but-simple 4-shape code (dot/line/triangle/circle); Indian participants included.
Design implications: Keep the code to a few simple, highly distinct shapes; make the mapping memorable (e.g., mnemonic consonance: line ~ fan blade?); provide a Braille/audio legend during learning.

Title: Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts
Authors: Ruxandra I. Tivadar; Benedetta Franceschiello; Astrid Minier; Micah M. Murray
Problem addressed: Whether a layout learned via a friction-based haptic tablet transfers to real navigation.
Target population: 25 normally sighted adults, tested blindfolded (no blind participants).
Methodology: Haptic exploration of an apartment floor plan (~45 min), LEGO reconstruction (Jaccard index), then blindfolded navigation on trained/untrained routes; permutation mixed ANOVAs.
Main findings: All reconstructions had Jaccard > 0.7, indicating layouts can be learned by touch; route training effects depended on group/route difficulty.
Limitations: Blindfolded sighted only; small groups; group confounded with route difficulty; one apartment.
Research gaps: Authors flag testing with blind/VI users as future work.
Relevance to SPARSH: Useful mainly as a methodological cautionary example: blindfolded sighted proxies are common but limit generalisation; also shows touch-learned spatial layouts can be retained.
Design implications: If SPARSH pilots with blindfolded students, label it as pilot/proxy evidence and confirm with blind users (see L42-L44).

Title: Experimental study about 3D printed tactile symbols for tactile maps and blind users
Authors: Jaume Gual Orti; Marina Puyuelo Cazorla; Joaquim Lloveras Macia; Javier Amat Cozar
Journal/conference: Journal of Accessibility and Design for All (JACCES), 14(2), 16-34 (published 11 Nov 2024)
Problem addressed: Whether volumetric (3D) symbols are recognised as well as conventional low-relief (2D) symbols.
Target population: 26 totally blind participants with varied tactile experience (Spain).
Methodology: Experiment; DV = % correct recognition; IV = volumetric vs low-relief form.
Main findings: Volumetric symbols showed high tactile recognition, comparable to 2D low-relief; 3D printing widens the usable symbol vocabulary beyond 2D-only rules.
Limitations: Symbol dimensions not verified (not in abstract/landing page); map context, not controls.
Research gaps: No studies of 3D tactile symbols mounted on switches/controls.
Relevance to SPARSH: Supports producing SPARSH caps as 3D-printed objects with volumetric (not just raised-line) shapes.
Design implications: Consider volumetric forms (e.g., dome for dot, ridge for line, pyramid/prism for triangle) for faster recognition.

Title: Applying height differentiation of tactile symbols to reduce the minimum horizontal distances between them on tactile maps
Authors: Jakub Wabinski; Emilia Smiechowska-Petrovskij; Albina Moscicka
Problem addressed: Tactile graphics need large gaps between symbols; can height differences let symbols sit closer?
Target population: 30 people with VI (16-65 y; 22 congenital/early blind), Poland.
Methodology: Within-subjects experiment on six 22x22 cm FDM/PLA pseudomaps; spacing 1, 2, 3 mm; uniform height 1.12 mm vs differentiated 0.56/1.12/1.68 mm (area/line/point).
Main findings: Without height differentiation, point-symbol task failed for 93.3% at 1 mm gap, success 36.7% at 2 mm and 56.7% at 3 mm; with height differentiation success 96.7% at all gaps and faster; minimum spacing could be cut from 3 mm to 1 mm.
Limitations: Single city sample; pseudomaps; FDM/PLA only; some non-significant comparisons; circle vs triangle/square confusions reported.
Research gaps: Not tested on curved/small surfaces like switch caps.
Relevance to SPARSH: Gives evidence-based heights for 3D-printed symbols (0.56-1.68 mm) and warns that circle/triangle/square can be confused at small sizes.
Design implications: Make the four SPARSH symbols differ in height/profile as well as outline (e.g., dot tallest); ensure triangle vs circle are large enough (>= 10 mm) to avoid confusion; >= 3 mm between raised elements if heights are equal.

Title: Tactile elevation perception in blind and sighted participants and its implications for tactile map creation
Authors: Sandra Jehoel; Paul T. Sowden; Simon Ungar; Annette Sterr
Problem addressed: Which symbol elevations are needed for tactile identification.
Target population: Sighted and visually impaired participants (n not verified).
Methodology: Two experiments: elevation vs identification accuracy; elevation and texture vs speed.
Main findings: Elevations of only ~0.040-0.080 mm sufficed for identification - far below the >= 0.5 mm common in tactile maps and 0.4 mm in guidelines; rough textures identified faster than smooth; VI participants outperformed sighted.
Limitations: Lab stimuli; sample details not verified.
Relevance to SPARSH: Shows that SPARSH's relief height is not limited by perception thresholds but by speed, durability and robustness to wear; also that VI users outperform sighted proxies.
Design implications: Choose height for speed/durability (0.5-1.5 mm) rather than minimum detectability; add texture to help discrimination; do not substitute sighted participants.

Title: TactIcons: Designing 3D Printed Map Icons for People who are Blind or have Low Vision
Authors: Leona Holloway; Matthew Butler; Kim Marriott
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23), pp. 1-18
Problem addressed: Visual map icons do not translate to touch.
Target population: Study 1: 46 (11 blind braille readers, 35 sighted); Study 2: 3 congenitally blind + 3 novice touch readers.
Methodology: Design of >200 3D-printed icons; touch-testing for instant recognition and learnability.
Main findings: 33 icons recognised instantly, 34 easy to learn; icons ~20 mm on 20 mm disc base, min component thickness 2 mm; guidelines: distinctive shapes (plain round/rectangular forms are hard to tell apart), important features at top, prefer 3D forms, raised outlines rather than indents, co-design with congenitally blind people, recognition varies by culture (e.g., power plugs).
Limitations: Map icons, not controls; heights not specified.
Relevance to SPARSH: Directly applicable icon-design guidance for SPARSH caps and a recommended touch-testing protocol (>= 3 congenitally blind + 3 novice testers).
Design implications: ~20 mm footprint if switch face allows; min 2 mm thick features; avoid indents/holes; test with congenitally blind and late-blind users; note cultural variation (Indian plug shapes differ).

Title: Accessible Maps for the Blind: Comparing 3D Printed Models with Tactile Graphics
Authors: Leona Holloway; Kim Marriott; Matthew Butler
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '18), pp. 1-13
Problem addressed: Whether 3D-printed models are better than raised-line tactile graphics for blind map reading.
Relevance to SPARSH: Frequently cited foundation for using 3D printing over 2D tactile graphics; cite only as background unless the team reads the paper.

Title: The Effect of Orientation on the Readability and Comfort of 3D-Printed Braille
Authors: Eduardo Puerta; Tarik Crnovrsanin; Laura South; Cody Dunne
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24), pp. 1-15
Problem addressed: FDM print orientation affects braille dot quality and comfort.
Methodology: Two mixed-methods studies (reading time, preference; sanded vs unsanded), thematic analysis; preregistered.
Main findings: Braille printed at 75 degrees and vertically was read faster and preferred over horizontal printing.
Limitations: Participant details and dot dimensions not verified.
Relevance to SPARSH: Print orientation matters for small raised features on FDM caps.
Design implications: Print small tactile features (dots) vertically/angled or with fine layer heights; consider sanding; prototype print orientation as a variable.
